Election week dominates the calendar — early voting ends Sunday 1–5 PM, then polls are open Tuesday 6:30 AM to 7:30 PM for the governor's race, the Husted–Brown Senate fight and every statewide office; note that 66 Cuyahoga precincts have moved, so check your location before Tuesday. items.title: Cavs vs Oklahoma City Thunder
A tanker is hit by limpet mines in Hormuz — the first attack of its kind since 2019
items.summary:
A small boat approached a tanker in the Strait of Hormuz on Thursday night and attached two explosive devices to its hull, about 25 nautical miles northeast of Khasab in Oman. The blasts set off an engine-room fire that was later put out, the crew stayed safe, and the ship — named in reporting as the Louise 1 — continued toward anchorage off the United Arab Emirates coast.

The incident sits alongside a wider set of Iranian claims. Iran's Revolutionary Guards said several tankers had hit mines or been halted after trying a southern route Tehran calls unauthorized, and Oman's maritime authorities said its navy evacuated 25 crew members from a Panama-flagged merchant ship that caught fire off Musandam. U.S. Central Command chief Admiral Brad Cooper said the main internationally recognized transit routes have been cleared of mines and that dozens of commercial vessels are moving through.

October has been the heaviest month for attacks on shipping since the war began in February, and the return of limpet mines — last used in the Gulf in 2019 — marks a change in tactics. The strait once carried about a fifth of the world's energy, so each new method of stopping ships raises the risk for crews and for oil prices, which have already pushed Brent toward $117 a barrel.

Watch for confirmation of which vessels were involved and whether more tankers pause or reroute in the next few days.

items.title: Spain works to identify 69 dead after a high-speed train was sent toward a stopped train
items.summary:
Spain is in a period of national mourning after two high-speed trains collided on Wednesday near Urda, in Toledo province, on the Madrid to Seville line. At least 69 people were killed and more than 100 were injured, and Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said people from as many as 27 countries may be among the victims. By Friday, all of the dead had undergone autopsies but only about half had been formally identified.

Transport Minister Óscar Puente said a failure in the LZB safety system stopped traffic along a long stretch of track, and a controller then authorized a Renfe train to proceed without speed limits. It accelerated to roughly 160 to 200 kilometers per hour before hitting a stationary Iryo train. Puente called the decision to restart traffic inexplicable and said the control center had time to check the error.

This is Spain's second major high-speed disaster this year, after a crash near Córdoba in January killed more than 40 people, and it has badly shaken trust in a network long held up as a European model. The minister has rejected calls to resign, and an independent investigation is still under way.

Watch for the investigation commission's findings on signaling and control-center procedures, and for identification updates for foreign victims, including an Oklahoma arts leader reported missing after the crash.

items.title: Israel's final election count leaves Netanyahu ahead — but eight seats short of governing
items.summary:
Final results from Israel's October 27 election give Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, ahead of the opposition bloc led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot with 48. Arab-led parties won an unprecedented 19 seats between them. Turnout reached 77.9 percent, the highest in decades.

No bloc reaches the 61 seats needed to govern, so the result points to weeks of coalition bargaining or possibly another election. Likud remains the largest single party with 27 seats, followed by Eisenkot's Yashar with 21. Election officials rejected claims of widespread fraud as baseless and said the vote was conducted lawfully, even as a security agency investigation into suspected foreign interference continues.

The deadlock matters beyond Israel because the next government will shape policy on Iran, Gaza and relations with Washington at a moment when the United States is also heading into its own midterms. The Arab parties now hold the balance, but both main blocs have historically been reluctant to rely on them to form a government.

The formal results go to Israel's president on November 4, and the lawmaker tapped to try first will have 28 days, plus a possible 14-day extension, to assemble a coalition. The new Knesset is due to be sworn in on November 10.

items.title: Congo's Ebola deaths pass 5,000, with cases now in Kenya, Nigeria and Uganda
items.summary:
Deaths in the Democratic Republic of Congo's Ebola outbreak have reached 5,026 among 10,351 confirmed infections, according to the latest health ministry figures released Saturday. That is a fatality rate near 50 percent, with 2,788 people recovered so far. The outbreak, declared in mid-May, has spread across 67 health zones in eight provinces, concentrated in Ituri and North Kivu.

The virus behind it is the Bundibugyo species, for which there is no approved vaccine or specific treatment, so care is supportive. About a third of deaths have occurred outside treatment centers, and health officials say most new infections are emerging outside known contact chains, which makes tracing far harder. Kenya has confirmed eight cases and two deaths, Nigeria has reported one case, and Uganda recorded cases earlier.

It is already the second-deadliest Ebola outbreak on record, behind only the 2014 to 2016 West Africa epidemic that killed more than 11,000 people, and the first to appear across three African regions at once. The United States has set travel restrictions tied to the outbreak starting November 3.

Watch for whether funding and staffing for contact tracing improve, and for any further cases outside Congo in the coming week.

items.title: Dockworkers strike at 113 ports in 22 countries over arms shipments and seafarers killed in war zones
items.summary:
Dockworkers walked out on Friday at 113 ports in 22 countries, disrupting shipping and ferry services in a coordinated protest against using civilian ports for arms shipments. Major hubs including Piraeus, Valencia, Le Havre, Algeciras and Genoa took part, along with Tangier Med in Morocco and Nhava Sheva in India. About 3,000 workers rallied at Piraeus alone, where island ferries were suspended.

More than 25 unions backed the action, which also pressed demands for pay rises, better conditions and doctors aboard vessels crossing war zones. Organizers pointed to 570 confirmed attacks in the Black Sea this year with 40 seafarers dead, and 28 attacks in the Gulf in the first 21 days of October alone. A campaign group involved said the protest could hold up some 52,000 containers worth about $2.8 billion, a figure Reuters could not independently verify.

The strike shows how wars at sea are landing on civilian workers far from the front lines, and it briefly snarled supply chains that are already strained by the Hormuz crisis.

Most actions were set for a day, so watch for whether unions call follow-up stoppages or win any commitments on military cargo.

items.title: China's factories shrink again in October as demand at home and for exports stays soft
items.summary:
China's official manufacturing purchasing managers' index fell to 49.3 in October from 50.1 in September, missing a forecast of 50.0 and marking the third contraction in four months. A reading below 50 signals shrinking activity. The separate index for services and construction also slipped, to 49.7 from 50.2.

The survey, released Saturday by the National Bureau of Statistics, pointed to soft demand for goods inside China and signs of weakness in export orders, with both new orders and new export orders staying in contraction. There were bright spots in high-end manufacturing: production and orders for railway, shipbuilding, aerospace and electronics equipment were all at or above 53.

As the world's largest manufacturer, a softer China ripples into commodity prices, shipping and the earnings of U.S. and European firms that sell there. It also adds pressure on Beijing to support growth heading into the final months of the year.

Watch for the private Caixin survey and for any new stimulus measures from Chinese policymakers in November.

items.title: Democrats take an 8-point lead into the final weekend, but the voters still to cast ballots are tied
items.summary:
Democrats go into the last weekend before Tuesday's midterms leading the generic congressional ballot 51.4 percent to 43.2 percent in the RealClearPolling average, an 8.2-point edge. All 435 House seats are up, Republicans currently hold 219 to Democrats' 214, and Democrats need a net gain of only three seats to take the House. In the Senate, 35 seats are contested and Democrats need a net gain of four to take control from a 53 to 47 Republican majority.

Forecasters see the House as the likelier flip: the Cook Political Report's range puts Democrats between 227 and 240 seats, and prediction markets on Friday gave Democrats about a 94 percent chance of winning the House and 69 percent for the Senate. Advertising spending for the cycle has reached $11.2 billion, a midterm record, and the cost of living remains voters' top concern. A final Cygnal poll adds a wrinkle — voters who have already cast ballots favor Democrats heavily, while those yet to vote split almost evenly and late deciders lean Republican.

President Trump's approval sits in the high 30s in recent polling, which has dragged on Republican candidates, but district-by-district results will decide control, not the national number.

Watch turnout over the final early-voting sessions this weekend and on Election Day itself, when more than half of the remaining vote is expected to be cast.

items.title: A judge bars the Justice Department from threatening election workers over ballots it calls ineligible
items.summary:
A federal judge in California issued an emergency order late Friday barring the Justice Department from threatening state and local election officials with criminal prosecution for counting ballots cast by registered voters the administration claims may be noncitizens. Labor unions and other groups had sued, arguing the threats could intimidate the people who run elections.

The order, from Judge Trina Thompson, runs through November 16, with another hearing set for November 13 — after Election Day. It arrives four days before midterms that will decide control of Congress, in a campaign already crowded with lawsuits over voter rolls and counting rules.

The ruling does not settle the underlying fight over eligibility checks. It does mean local officials can administer Tuesday's vote without the immediate risk of prosecution for following their normal procedures, which both sides will be watching closely in close races.

Watch for an administration appeal and for any similar challenges filed in other states over the weekend.

items.title: Four days before the election, the Justice Department opens a probe of Arizona voter registration groups
items.summary:
The Justice Department announced Friday that it is investigating the Arizona voter registration work of three Democratic-aligned groups, after an undercover video purported to show volunteers willing to register noncitizens. The announcement landed four days before the November 3 election.

The probe adds Arizona — a perennial battleground with tight House and Senate races — to a growing list of election-administration fights playing out in the campaign's final days. Registration groups are a routine part of turnout operations for both parties, and investigations announced this close to a vote tend to draw sharp reactions about timing and intent.

No charges were announced with the investigation, and the groups' responses will shape how much this becomes a voting issue versus a campaign issue in the state's closing stretch.

Watch for statements from the organizations named, from Arizona election officials, and for any court filings before Tuesday.

items.title: Federal raids in Minnesota: 17 warrants in a day and four arrests in an alleged $41 million health-care fraud
items.summary:
FBI Director Kash Patel and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent traveled to Minnesota on Friday to announce 17 anti-fraud search warrants executed in a single day and four arrests tied to a 26-count indictment. Prosecutors allege the defendants tried to steal $41 million from federal health programs, with actual losses estimated at about $21.65 million.

Those charged include operators of autism services, home health and therapy businesses, facing counts of health-care fraud and conspiracy. Three warrants hit a child care center and others hit owners' homes and a behavioral-intervention unit. Separately, the Justice Department said cases charged, convicted or sentenced in the past month involve nearly $83 million in intended losses, and investigators have issued more than 1,000 subpoenas in Minnesota this year.

Bessent sharply criticized former Governor Tim Walz's administration as negligent on fraud, making the enforcement push a political as well as a criminal story days before the midterms. All defendants are presumed innocent unless proven guilty.

Watch for arraignments, for any further arrests, and for how Minnesota's state races handle the fraud issue in the final days.

items.title: The administration plans to deport some Afghan immigrants to Afghanistan, via Pakistan
items.summary:
The Trump administration plans to deport some Afghan immigrants to Afghanistan, a U.S. official and a coalition of veterans and advocacy groups said Friday. Many of those facing removal fled after the Taliban takeover and the U.S. withdrawal in 2021, according to Shawn VanDiver, head of the #AfghanEvac coalition.

More than 150 Afghan immigrants are expected to be removed, the New York Times reported, which would make it one of the largest single expulsions of Afghans. Dozens have been detained in Louisiana, and a first flight could leave as soon as Monday. Because Washington has no diplomatic ties with the Taliban, a U.S. official said deportations would be routed via Pakistan. The Homeland Security Department declined to confirm future operations, citing operational security.

The plan is likely to draw intense scrutiny because many Afghans who assisted or were associated with the U.S. effort fear Taliban retaliation, and veterans' groups have been among the loudest advocates for keeping pathways open for them.

Watch for court challenges over the weekend and for confirmation of any flight on Monday.

items.title: The G20 scraps its family photo rather than pose its ministers next to Russia's Lavrov
items.summary:
The G20 foreign ministers' meeting in Atlanta opened Friday without its traditional family photo, after more than a third of attending officials were expected to walk out rather than be pictured alongside Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, the host, explored taking two photos — one with Lavrov and one without — before scrapping the photo altogether.

Germany's foreign minister said there could be no joint photo because there is no normality with Russia, and Britain's foreign secretary said the U.K. does not engage with Russia that way. Lavrov dismissed the episode as family-photo diplomacy and said he had a fairly good brief conversation with Rubio. U.S. officials said they dropped the photo to keep a ceremonial moment from becoming a spectacle that overshadowed the talks.

The cancellation is a small moment with a large signal: four years into the Ukraine war, the forum built for the world's biggest economies cannot produce its most basic image of unity, and the meeting is expected to end with a chair's statement rather than a joint communiqué.

Leaders meet in Miami on December 14 and 15 for the summit that closes the U.S. G20 presidency — watch whether the same split follows them there.

items.title: The AI selloff gets worse: Nasdaq's biggest drop since June, Intel down about 29 percent
items.summary:
U.S. stocks closed sharply lower on Friday as disappointing results from Intel and Amazon deepened doubts about how quickly enormous artificial-intelligence spending will pay off. The Nasdaq Composite fell 2.86 percent to 25,437, its biggest one-day drop since June 5, the S&P 500 fell 1.82 percent, and the Dow fell 1.09 percent. The Nasdaq is now down 7.8 percent from its October 6 record close.

Intel plunged about 29 percent on a weak outlook tied to softer computer demand. Nvidia fell about 4 percent, AMD about 11 percent, and the broader semiconductor index dropped 7.2 percent, taking its monthly loss past 15 percent. Server makers Dell and HP fell roughly 10 percent each. Defensive names held up better, with Walmart and Coca-Cola each rising more than 1 percent. Even so, about 82 percent of S&P 500 companies reporting so far have beaten earnings estimates, with expected quarterly growth above 30 percent.

The split picture — strong reported profits, punished AI spenders — is the story of this earnings season, and it is now moving the whole market, not just tech.

Watch Monday's open after the weekend, and whether midterm results on Tuesday calm or extend the rotation out of growth stocks.

items.title: Binance says withdrawals should restart in phases around November 1, with $6.34 billion set aside to cover the hack
items.summary:
Binance has set aside more than $6.34 billion to cover the roughly $6.3 billion stolen from its wallets on October 29, its co-chief executives said in an October 30 update, including about $5 billion held in the same tokens that were taken. Blockchain firm TRM Labs traced about $6.36 billion moving across ten blockchains, most of it in about 20 minutes, and attributes the theft to TraderTraitor, the North Korean group the FBI blamed for last year's $1.5 billion Bybit hack.

About $3 billion has been frozen on-chain with partners — Tether froze more than $1.5 billion in USDT and Circle more than $800 million in USDC — while TRM estimates the attacker still controls roughly $2.4 billion. Binance says the breach began with a compromised engineer's laptop that let the attacker submit unauthorized withdrawals, and it reports no evidence of a private-key leak. The FBI and the Secret Service are both involved.

Withdrawals have been paused since the theft while deposits still work. Binance aims to resume withdrawals in phases within about 34 hours of its Friday update, which points to the early hours of November 1, followed by a new proof-of-reserves snapshot by November 2 and a full technical post-mortem.

Watch for whether withdrawals actually restart on that timetable — the clearest test of whether users believe the exchange's cover pledge.

items.title: OpenAI trims its funding target by $10 billion as the tech rout reaches private markets
items.summary:
OpenAI has cut the target for its latest funding round by $10 billion, the Financial Times reported Friday, and is now seeking about $20 billion at a valuation of $1.25 trillion, down from $30 billion at $1.4 trillion last month. The company set a Friday deadline for investor commitments, but the first close is expected to come in below $20 billion after some investors reduced their allocations.

A consortium of United Arab Emirates investors including state-backed fund MGX is expected to be the largest participant, with a deal that could give OpenAI the option to lease new computing capacity in the region. Founders Fund, Coatue, Sequoia Capital and Andreessen Horowitz are also expected to take part, and wealthy individuals may get a later retail offering at the same valuation. None of the firms commented to Reuters.

OpenAI is pursuing a listing in 2027 and wants to close ahead of rival Anthropic's imminent public offering, since both are courting the same investors. The cut shows the public-market AI selloff is now repricing even the most sought-after private names.

Watch for the actual first-close figure and for Anthropic's debut pricing, which will set the comparison.

items.title: DoorDash to buy Instacart for $17 billion — and one membership would cover both
items.summary:
DoorDash announced Thursday it will acquire Instacart for about $17 billion, or $65 a share, a 26 percent premium to Instacart's closing price on October 22, before deal reports surfaced. At least 75 percent of the price will be cash, funded from DoorDash's reserves and new debt backed by a bridge facility from JPMorgan Chase, with the rest available in DoorDash stock.

The companies say Instacart shoppers would gain access to more than 50,000 additional stores on top of the roughly 100,000 already on the platform, and people holding both DashPass and Instacart+ would pay a single membership fee — a saving DoorDash estimates at $100 million a year for customers. DoorDash plans to keep Instacart's brand, app and the technology it sells to grocers, and says local grocers will stay free to work with any delivery platform.

An anti-monopoly group has already urged regulators to block the deal, arguing it would control nearly 60 percent of third-party grocery delivery. Closing is not expected until late 2027 or the first half of 2028, after shareholder and antitrust approvals in the U.S., Canada and Israel.

Watch the regulatory review — its timeline will decide whether the combined company ever operates as pitched.

items.title: Big Tech's $740 billion spending year is eating its cash flow — and investors have noticed
items.summary:
Earnings from Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Microsoft this month put hard numbers on the AI build-out: the four outlined capital spending plans totaling more than $740 billion this year, and three of the four reported negative free cash flow for the period. Alphabet burned $9.1 billion with capex guidance up to $205 billion, Amazon is at negative $42.4 billion over twelve months with a $220 billion plan, and Meta burned $2.1 billion in the quarter. Only Microsoft stayed cash-positive, at $18.6 billion.

Together with Oracle, the group has raised about $326 billion in debt in 2026, triple last year's pace. The market response has been severe: the Nasdaq briefly entered correction territory in October, Alphabet had its worst day on record, and heavily leveraged newer cloud firms fell 35 percent or more in the month.

The companies argue demand for computing still outruns supply and that cloud revenue is growing fast — Google Cloud is closing on Azure and AWS revenue rose 39 percent. The argument investors are making back is simpler: show the returns.

Watch capex guidance in the next round of calls and whether any major firm trims a data-center plan, which would be the first real break in the build-out.
items.source: Axios and TechCrunch via Zot News

items.title: As tech slides, money rotates to defensives — and Anthropic's debut gets a cooler reception
items.summary:
Friday's trading showed a clear rotation: while chip and cloud names fell hard, Walmart and Coca-Cola each gained more than 1 percent and drugmakers Merck and Amgen also advanced, cushioning the Dow's decline relative to the Nasdaq. For October as a whole, the Nasdaq fell 5.3 percent, its steepest monthly drop since March 2025.

Sentiment took another hit from a report that Blackstone had told investors Anthropic may not secure an investment-grade rating at its debut, softening the optimism that followed the AI firm's S-1 filing earlier in the week. Smaller AI-linked funds fell sharply in the month, including a memory-chip fund down about 20 percent and an AI innovation fund down nearly 17 percent, and newer cloud operators CoreWeave and Nebius lost roughly a third of their value.

Rotation into defensives ahead of an election week is a classic risk-off signal, and it suggests fund managers want steadier cash flows until both earnings and politics clear.

Watch whether defensive strength persists after Tuesday, or whether a clean election result pulls money back into growth.

items.title: The manhunt for an escaped Tennessee murderer enters its sixth day, with the reward now at $17,500
items.summary:
Jacob Allen Morley, 28, serving a life sentence for first-degree murder, was discovered missing from the Northwest Correctional Complex in Lake County late on October 25. Security video showed him breaching the perimeter fence in his prison uniform, and footage from about 1 a.m. on October 26 showed him taking a white 2008 Ford F-350 from a nearby farm business.

The truck was found abandoned on October 27 in Marion, Illinois, about 120 miles north, with no sign of Morley. The Tennessee Bureau of Investigation has placed him on its Most Wanted list and asked residents to check doorbell and trail cameras. The reward has climbed in steps to $17,500, with contributions from the governor, the U.S. Marshals Service and TBI itself.

Morley is the second person to escape Tennessee corrections custody in about a week, and the escape came in the same month the department's commissioner resigned after a failed execution left a prisoner on a ventilator. Authorities describe Morley as 5 feet 11 inches and 240 pounds with brown hair and green eyes, and say anyone who sees him should call 911 and not approach.

Watch for any confirmed sighting — so far, investigators in Illinois say he appears to have vanished after leaving the truck.

items.title: Pope Leo XIV submits his Chicago mail ballot — a first for a sitting pope
items.summary:
Pope Leo XIV has submitted a mail-in ballot for the U.S. midterms, the Vatican confirmed Friday, making him the first pope to vote in a U.S. election and likely the first to vote in a secular democratic election at all. The Chicago-born pope, elected in May 2025, is registered under his birth name, Robert Francis Prevost, at an address in New Lenox, Illinois, where his brother lives, and he requested his ballot on October 3.

His Illinois ballot covers the race to succeed retiring Senator Dick Durbin, Governor JB Pritzker's bid for a third term, and House, state and county contests. The Vatican said Leo has voted whenever eligible throughout his life, including during his years in Peru, and framed the ballot as a belief in the right and duty of citizens to take part in democratic processes. It did not say how he voted.

Historians note the novelty plainly: no previous pope held citizenship in a democracy where he could cast such a ballot while in office.

Leo begins a tour of Latin America on November 6 — watch for whether his civic example becomes a theme of that trip.

items.title: A Texas grand jury indicts an ICE officer accused of striking a fleeing man with his SUV
items.summary:
A Harris County grand jury has indicted ICE officer Mario Alberto Morales, 33, on a charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon, a second-degree felony carrying two to twenty years in prison. Prosecutors say that on October 10 in northwest Houston, Morales drove an unmarked Jeep Grand Cherokee over a median and struck Miguel Parra-Hernandez, 48, a Mexican construction worker who was running on foot during an enforcement operation, breaking his leg in several places.

District Attorney Sean Teare released body-camera and surveillance video on Friday and said it contradicts ICE's account that Parra-Hernandez ran in front of the vehicle. In the body-camera audio, Morales acknowledges hitting him with the car. Morales's attorney calls the collision a tragic accident, and ICE calls the indictment a political stunt and denies any intentional strike. Morales was not yet in custody Friday, and a warrant is to be issued.

Prosecutors and commentators describe the case as the first attempt to criminally prosecute an ICE officer in Texas, and a rare state prosecution of a federal officer during the current immigration crackdown. Federal officials criticized the indictment and said their own review found no basis for federal charges, which are separate from the state case.

Watch for Morales's surrender or arrest, and for a possible fight over moving the case to federal court.

items.title: King tides ease this weekend — but forecasters warn Thanksgiving week could flood both coasts again
items.summary:
October's king tides produced record flood levels in Southern California, including Los Angeles and San Diego, flooding roads and beachfront property, while Virginia Key near Miami recorded moderate flooding for a record ten straight days at levels topped only during hurricanes Irma and Wilma. In Florida's Treasure Coast, advisories continued through Saturday's high tide even as the peak passed.

Forecasters say the next round arrives over Thanksgiving week with the next full moon, and California's tides then could run about half a foot higher than October's highest. Warm ocean water and an El Niño-driven bulge of water against the West Coast are adding to the astronomical tide, and similar rounds are expected around Christmas and again in late January.

King tides are a preview of ordinary future sea levels, which is why coastal cities track them so closely: the places that flood now, on a sunny day with no storm, are the places that will flood routinely.

Watch the Thanksgiving forecasts for California and Florida, especially if onshore winds or a storm coincide with the highest tides.

items.title: Halloween night looks dry and mild for most of the East, wet for parts of the West and Plains
items.summary:
Trick-or-treaters across the Northeast and Great Lakes can expect a dry, mild evening under high pressure, with temperatures in the 50s and 60s across much of the Midwest and East. It is the last night of daylight saving time — clocks fall back early Sunday, the earliest possible date for the change.

The trouble spots are elsewhere: showers and thunderstorms are possible across Texas and the Plains and from Arkansas and Louisiana toward the Carolinas, much of the West may see rain, and parts of the Rockies and Sierra Nevada could see snow. San Diego may record its first measurable Halloween rain in 39 years. The coldest conditions will be in Montana, Idaho, Wyoming and the inland Northwest, where feels-like temperatures could sit in the 30s and 40s.

For Solon, the local outlook matches the favorable eastern pattern — cloudy and dry, with evening temperatures expected in the low to mid-50s for the 6 to 8 p.m. trick-or-treat window.

Sunday brings a pattern change for parts of the country, so check local forecasts before any outdoor plans tomorrow.

items.title: An Oklahoma arts leader is missing after Spain's train crash, and his family is asking for help
items.summary:
Fernando Calvillo, 45, community relations director of the Oklahoma Visual Arts Coalition, is missing after Wednesday's high-speed train collision in Spain. He was traveling on the Madrid to Seville line with his husband, Lawrence Naff, who is hospitalized and recovering from his injuries.

The crash killed at least 69 people and is Spain's worst rail disaster since 2013. Calvillo's family says they have not been able to confirm his whereabouts amid an identification process that, two days on, had formally identified only about half of the victims.

The case is a reminder that the Toledo province wreck reached far beyond Spain — officials believe victims came from as many as 27 countries — and that identification, not rescue, is now the painful work for many families.

The family asks anyone with information to contact the numbers they have shared publicly through Oklahoma news outlets, and says they will update through those channels.

items.title: Acton and Ramaswamy make their final pitches in a governor's race that turned personal
items.summary:
Democrat Amy Acton and Republican Vivek Ramaswamy spent the final days of Ohio's governor's race making sharply different closing arguments. Acton, who led the state health department during the pandemic, is pitching fully funded public schools and tax breaks for working Ohioans, telling supporters in Dayton that it is time for change after decades of Republican control. Ramaswamy, backed by President Trump, is promising to eliminate the state income tax, roll back property taxes and investigate every locality where property taxes have more than doubled since before the pandemic.

The race has been defined as much by a bitter advertising fight — including a Ramaswamy ad featuring Acton's estranged mother that his campaign later shortened and stopped emphasizing — as by policy. Polling averages give Acton a lead of roughly three to four points, and both the Cook Political Report and Sabato's Crystal Ball moved the race to Lean Democratic in late October, though partisan polls still show a dead heat and Ramaswamy's side has outspent Acton's by about three to one.

Ohio has not elected a Democratic governor since Ted Strickland, who left office in 2011, and the state voted for Trump by eleven points in 2024 — which makes Acton's polling lead the surprise of the cycle.

Polls are open Tuesday from 6:30 a.m. to 7:30 p.m. Watch Cuyahoga County turnout, where Democrats need a strong showing to hold any statewide lead.

items.title: A judge puts Glenville back in the playoffs — and University School says it may not play
items.summary:
The Ohio High School Athletic Association said late Friday it will comply with a court order requiring Glenville's playoff game against University School to be played, after a Cuyahoga County judge granted the Tarblooders a temporary restraining order. OHSAA had removed Glenville from the Division III playoffs on Thursday after an audit of student residency information, a ruling the association says it stands by.

Attorneys for Ginn Academy student-athletes filed the motion Friday, and Judge Andrew Santoli granted it the same day. The game was planned for today at noon, but reports say University School may not take part. OHSAA said it first requested residency records from Cleveland Metropolitan School District on September 28, received an initial batch on October 22, and met with Glenville on October 29, where the school did not object to the audit's findings.

Glenville, 8-2 this season, won the Division IV state title last year and is chasing its fourth championship in five years, so the ruling decides whether a title defense happens at all.

A hearing is scheduled for Monday — watch for whether the game is actually played this weekend and what Monday's hearing means for the rest of the bracket.

items.title: Guardians protect shortstop Milan Tolentino on the 40-man roster and decline two bullpen options
items.summary:
The Cleveland Guardians selected the contract of 24-year-old shortstop Milan Tolentino from Triple-A Columbus, adding him to the 40-man roster. The move protects the left-handed hitter from the Rule 5 draft and keeps him from reaching minor-league free agency.

Tolentino, a fourth-round pick in 2020, hit .225 with a .328 on-base percentage and .453 slugging for Columbus in 2026, with 21 home runs, 74 RBIs and about 20 stolen bases across roughly 497 plate appearances, alongside a high strikeout total. He is valued more for power, patience and defensive versatility than for prospect rankings, and he is not expected to open next season as a starter.

The same day, Cleveland declined its club option on reliever Trevor Stephan and its half of a mutual option on Shawn Armstrong, leaving the 40-man roster at 36 and opening early questions about how the bullpen will be rebuilt.

Cleveland has reached the ALCS in two of the last three seasons — watch the option and non-tender deadlines ahead for more roster shaping.

items.title: Browns get Graham and Hall back together up front — but the right tackle spot is in doubt for Pittsburgh
items.summary:
Cleveland's defensive line news is good heading into Sunday's first-place showdown at Pittsburgh: Mason Graham is back in the lineup and Mike Hall Jr., who suffered a high ankle sprain against the Steelers on October 1, is off the injury report and will play. Head coach Todd Monken welcomed Hall's return for a defense that has battled injuries up front all season, with Kalia Davis already out for the year.

The worry is on the other side of the ball. Starting right tackle Tytus Howard, who suffered a concussion in the win over Tennessee, missed all three practices this week and is listed as questionable, along with cornerback Myles Harden and safety Daniel Thomas, who has an ankle injury. Dawand Jones has worked with the first team all week and would step in if Howard cannot clear the concussion protocol.

At 5-2, the Browns can take sole possession of first place in the AFC North with a win — and end a regular-season losing streak in Pittsburgh that stretches back to 2003.

Kickoff is Sunday at 1 p.m. on CBS. Watch the final inactive list about ninety minutes before the game for Howard's status.

items.title: Sunday in Pittsburgh is Cleveland's chance to end a 22-game road losing streak to the Steelers
items.summary:
The Browns' visit to Pittsburgh on Sunday is being framed around the franchise as its biggest game in years, because a win would do two things at once: put 5-2 Cleveland alone in first place in the AFC North and end a regular-season road losing streak to the Steelers that dates to 2003 — 22 straight losses in Pittsburgh.

Much of the local focus is on quarterback Deshaun Watson, whose strong first seven weeks have rewritten his own story this season and who helped beat Pittsburgh earlier this year. Cleveland.com's Dan Labbe wrote this week about how much the game means for Watson and for a team run by many new faces who had nothing to do with those 22 losses. A subplot to watch is cornerback Denzel Ward, who has already intercepted Aaron Rodgers once this year and, by local reporting, wants Rodgers throwing his way again.

Even a loss leaves Cleveland in a strong playoff position, which is part of why players and coaches are treating the game as opportunity rather than pressure.

One logistical quirk: Pitt hosts Georgia Tech in the same stadium tonight, giving crews an unusually tight turnaround before Sunday's 1 p.m. kickoff — a detail Browns safety Grant Delpit joked about while blaming the field for past struggles.

items.title: Final weekend of early voting in Ohio: today until 4, Sunday 1 to 5 — then Tuesday decides it
items.summary:
Early in-person voting is open today, Saturday, from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. across Ohio, and for a final session Sunday from 1 to 5 p.m., before Election Day on Tuesday, November 3, when polls run 6:30 a.m. to 7:30 p.m. Nearly a million Ohio ballots had already been returned by October 23, in a midterm that will decide the governor's race, the Husted-Brown Senate contest, every statewide office and two seats on the Ohio Supreme Court.

Cuyahoga County voters should double-check their Election Day location before Tuesday: 66 precincts in the county have moved. The statewide ballot also includes Issue 3, a proposed constitutional amendment requiring photo identification at the polls. In Cleveland today, voting itself is getting a Halloween twist, with a Pull Up to the Polls block party outside the Cuyahoga County Board of Elections from 11:30 a.m. to 2 p.m.

After Sunday, the only way to vote is in person on Tuesday — absentee ballots must also be handled under Ohio's return deadlines, so anyone still holding one should check the county board's guidance today rather than Monday.

Watch turnout reports from the Secretary of State over the weekend for a final read on which side banked more early votes.

baby.tip: Do the final hospital-bag sweep together this weekend: IDs and insurance cards in the front pocket, phone chargers and a long cable, snacks for Mike, and a going-home outfit for the baby in newborn and 0–3 month sizes — babies pick their own size. Then leave the bag by the door, not in a closet, so nobody is packing at 3 AM.
baby.fact: Newborns see best at about 8 to 12 inches from their face — almost exactly the distance to a parent's face during a feed — and they already recognize their mother's voice from hearing it in the womb. High-contrast black-and-white patterns are the first 'pictures' a new baby can really study.
